questions.stem: What are the three parts of a DNA nucleotide?
options: A deoxyribose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base
A ribose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base such as uracil
A deoxyribose sugar, an amino acid and a phosphate group
A glucose molecule, a fatty acid and a nitrogenous base
questions.explanation: Each DNA nucleotide has deoxyribose, a phosphate and one of the bases A, T, G or C. Ribose is the sugar in RNA nucleotides, not DNA.

questions.stem: Which base pairs form in a DNA double helix?
options: Adenine with uracil, and guanine with cytosine
Adenine with thymine, and guanine with cytosine
Adenine with guanine, and thymine with cytosine
Adenine with cytosine, and guanine with thymine
questions.explanation: Complementary base pairing joins A to T and G to C across the two strands. Uracil replaces thymine only in RNA.

questions.stem: A sample of double-stranded DNA contains 18% cytosine. What percentage of its bases are adenine?
questions.explanation: Cytosine pairs with guanine, so G = 18% and C + G = 36%. The remaining 64% is split equally between A and T, giving 32% adenine.

questions.stem: A ten base-pair section of DNA has 4 A-T pairs and 6 G-C pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold the two strands together in this section?
questions.explanation: A-T pairs are held by 2 hydrogen bonds and G-C pairs by 3, so 4 × 2 + 6 × 3 = 8 + 18 = 26. Assuming 2 bonds per pair gives 20.

questions.stem: What does it mean that the two strands of a DNA double helix are antiparallel?
options: They run in opposite directions, one 5' to 3' and the other 3' to 5'
They are joined by covalent bonds between the bases on each of the strands
They have identical base sequences, so either one can be copied
They never pair up with each other again once they are separated
questions.explanation: One strand runs 5' to 3' and its partner runs 3' to 5', which affects how DNA polymerase can copy each strand. The strands are complementary, not identical, and the bases are joined by hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: Why are the bases on the inside of the double helix and the sugar-phosphate backbones on the outside?
options: The backbones are made of hydrophobic fatty acids, so they must face away from the bases
The bases are much larger than the backbone, so they must fill the middle of the helix
The backbones are hydrophilic and face the water, while the paired bases are stacked inside
The bases need to be on the inside because they are the only parts that can bond to proteins
questions.explanation: The charged phosphate and polar sugar groups interact with water on the outside, while the flat bases stack in the centre, paired by hydrogen bonds. DNA contains no fatty acids.

questions.stem: At the replication fork, what does the enzyme helicase do?
options: It makes the short RNA primer that is needed to start each new strand
It adds new DNA nucleotides to the growing strand opposite the template
It unwinds the double helix and breaks the hydrogen bonds between bases
It joins short fragments of DNA by sealing the sugar-phosphate backbone
questions.explanation: Helicase separates the two strands at the replication fork so each can act as a template. Joining fragments is ligase's job, primers are made by primase, and nucleotides are added by DNA polymerase.

questions.stem: Why is primase needed during DNA replication?
options: The template strand must be destroyed after copying, so primase breaks it down into nucleotides
DNA polymerase cannot start a new strand, so primase lays down a short RNA primer to build from
Helicase cannot break hydrogen bonds by itself, so primase supplies it with the energy needed
Ligase cannot join DNA fragments together, so primase makes the bonds between Okazaki fragments
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to an existing strand end, so primase makes a short RNA primer to begin each new strand or fragment. The primers are later replaced with DNA.

questions.stem: In which direction does DNA polymerase build a new DNA strand?
options: 5' to 3', adding nucleotides to the 3' end of the growing strand
3' to 5', adding nucleotides to the 5' end of the growing strand
In both directions at once, outwards from the primer in the middle
In whichever direction the helicase happens to be moving that time
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the free 3' end, so new strands always grow 5' to 3'. This is why one strand at each fork must be made in fragments.

questions.stem: How is the lagging strand made during DNA replication?
options: In short Okazaki fragments, each built away from the fork and then joined by ligase
Continuously in one long piece, built towards the replication fork as it opens
By copying the leading strand after it is complete, using it as the template
In short fragments made by helicase, which are later joined together end to end by primase
questions.explanation: Because polymerase works only 5' to 3', the strand oriented the other way is made in short pieces, each started by a primer. Ligase joins these Okazaki fragments into one continuous strand.

questions.stem: What is the role of DNA ligase in replication?
options: Laying down short RNA primers on the template strand for polymerase to extend
Checking new strands for wrongly paired bases and cutting them out
Joining Okazaki fragments by sealing gaps in the sugar-phosphate backbone
Breaking hydrogen bonds so that the two template strands can separate
questions.explanation: After primers are replaced with DNA, small gaps remain in the backbone between fragments; ligase forms the bonds that seal them. Breaking hydrogen bonds is helicase's role.

questions.stem: A replication fork is opening from left to right. Template strand X runs 3' to 5' from left to right. How is the new strand built on template X?
options: Continuously, as the lagging strand, growing away from the fork
In fragments, as the leading strand, growing towards the fork
Continuously, as the leading strand, growing towards the fork
In fragments, as the lagging strand, growing away from the fork
questions.explanation: The new strand is antiparallel to X, so it runs 5' to 3' from left to right, the same direction the fork opens. Polymerase can follow the fork continuously, making this the leading strand.

questions.stem: Why is DNA replication described as semi-conservative?
options: Half of the genes in the cell are copied while the other half are conserved
Each new DNA molecule contains two new strands, and the old molecule is kept
The new strands contain half DNA nucleotides and half RNA nucleotides
Each new DNA molecule contains one original strand and one newly made strand
questions.explanation: Each original strand acts as a template and stays paired with its new complementary strand. A conservative model, now rejected, would keep the original double helix intact alongside a wholly new one.

questions.stem: Bacteria grown for many generations with heavy nitrogen (¹⁵N) are moved to normal nitrogen (¹⁴N) and allowed to replicate their DNA twice. If replication is semi-conservative, what DNA is expected after the second round?
options: Half heavy ¹⁵N DNA and half light ¹⁴N DNA
One quarter heavy ¹⁵N DNA and three quarters light
Half hybrid ¹⁵N-¹⁴N DNA and half light ¹⁴N DNA
All hybrid ¹⁵N-¹⁴N DNA and no light ¹⁴N DNA
questions.explanation: After round one every molecule is hybrid. In round two each hybrid separates: the ¹⁵N strand pairs with a new ¹⁴N strand (hybrid) and the ¹⁴N strand pairs with a new ¹⁴N strand (light), giving half and half. No fully heavy DNA remains after round one.

questions.stem: Students model DNA replication with paper strips for nucleotides. Which is a limitation of this model?
options: It cannot show the helix unwinding or the enzymes working as proteins at the fork
It cannot show complementary base pairing between the two strands of the model
It cannot show that each new molecule keeps one of the original paper strands
It cannot show that the bases A, T, G and C are different from each other
questions.explanation: A flat paper model shows complementary pairing and semi-conservative copying well, but not the three-dimensional twisting, the speed of replication or the enzymes as molecules. The other features are exactly what such models show clearly.

questions.stem: How does DNA usually exist in a bacterial cell?
options: As many linear chromosomes inside a membrane-bound nucleus
As linear chromosomes wound around histones in the cytoplasm
As short strands of RNA attached to the inside of the cell wall
As one circular chromosome in the nucleoid, often with small plasmids
questions.explanation: Bacteria have a single circular chromosome, not enclosed by a membrane, and many also carry plasmids. Several linear chromosomes in a nucleus is the eukaryotic arrangement.

questions.stem: Which comparison of DNA in eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells is correct?
options: Eukaryotic DNA is single-stranded; bacterial DNA is double-stranded and wound around histones
Eukaryotic nuclear DNA is linear and wound around histones; bacterial DNA is circular and not
Eukaryotic nuclear DNA is circular and free in the cytoplasm; bacterial DNA is linear in a nucleus
Eukaryotic cells have no circular DNA at all; bacterial cells have no linear or circular DNA
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic chromosomes are linear DNA molecules packaged with histone proteins in the nucleus. Bacterial chromosomes are circular and not packaged around histones.

questions.stem: Apart from the nucleus, where else is DNA found in a plant leaf cell?
options: In the cell wall and vacuole, as strands wound around histones
In the cell membrane, as plasmids attached to the glycoproteins
In the mitochondria and chloroplasts, as small circular molecules
In the Golgi body and ribosomes, as short linear molecules
questions.explanation: Mitochondria and chloroplasts each contain their own small circular DNA, similar to bacterial DNA. Ribosomes contain RNA, not DNA, and the wall and vacuole hold no DNA.

questions.stem: How do somatic cells and gametes differ in humans?
options: Somatic cells contain only autosomes; gametes contain only sex chromosomes
Somatic cells are diploid (46 chromosomes); gametes are haploid (23 chromosomes)
Somatic cells are haploid (23 chromosomes); gametes are diploid (46 chromosomes)
Somatic cells have no nucleus; gametes have a nucleus with 46 chromosomes
questions.explanation: Body (somatic) cells have two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent, while sperm and eggs have one set, so fertilisation restores 46. Gametes carry 22 autosomes and one sex chromosome.

questions.stem: Why is a mutation in a gametic cell more significant for future generations than one in a somatic cell?
options: A somatic mutation is always repaired straight away, but a gamete cannot repair any DNA
A gamete contains twice as much DNA as a somatic cell, so the mutation is copied twice
A gamete can pass the mutation to offspring, but a somatic mutation stays in the individual
A gamete divides much faster than a somatic cell, so its mutations spread right through the body
questions.explanation: Only DNA in gametes is passed to offspring, so a germline mutation can be inherited. A somatic mutation may affect the individual, for example as a cancer, but is not inherited.

questions.stem: Which feature of a human egg cell relates to its role?
options: It has many mitochondria in a midpiece to power its movement towards the sperm
It is large and contains stored nutrients and cytoplasm for the early embryo
It has a long flagellum that propels it rapidly through the oviduct to the sperm
It contains 46 chromosomes so that it can develop without being fertilised
questions.explanation: The egg supplies the cytoplasm, organelles and nutrients for the first divisions of the embryo. The flagellum and mitochondria-packed midpiece belong to the sperm, and the egg is haploid.

questions.stem: What happens during the G1 phase of the cell cycle?
options: The sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles
The cytoplasm divides to form two separate daughter cells
The cell grows, makes proteins and produces more organelles
The DNA is copied so each chromosome has two sister chromatids
questions.explanation: G1 (gap 1) is a period of growth and normal cell activity. DNA is replicated in the S phase, chromatids separate in anaphase of mitosis, and the cytoplasm divides in cytokinesis.

questions.stem: A cell has a certain mass of DNA in G1. How much DNA does it contain at the end of the S phase, and how much will each daughter cell have after mitosis and cytokinesis?
options: Four times the G1 amount; then twice the G1 amount
Twice the G1 amount; then the same amount as in G1
The same as in G1; then half the G1 amount
Twice the G1 amount; then half the G1 amount
questions.explanation: Replication in the S phase doubles the DNA. Mitosis shares it equally, so each daughter cell returns to the G1 amount. Halving the DNA content is what meiosis does.

questions.stem: What is the main purpose of the G2 phase?
options: Replication of the DNA, so each chromosome is made up of two chromatids
Pairing of homologous chromosomes so that crossing over can take place
Division of the cytoplasm after the nuclear membrane has re-formed
Further growth and preparation for mitosis, including checking the copied DNA
questions.explanation: In G2 the cell continues to grow, makes proteins needed for division and checks that DNA replication was complete and accurate. Pairing of homologues happens only in meiosis.

questions.stem: In a sample of 300 root tip cells, 30 are in mitosis. If the cell cycle takes 24 hours, about how long does mitosis last?
options: 2.4 hours
10 hours
0.8 hours
7.2 hours
questions.explanation: The fraction of cells in mitosis estimates the fraction of the cycle spent in it: 30 ÷ 300 = 0.1, and 0.1 × 24 h = 2.4 h. Dividing 300 by 30 gives 10, which is not a time.

questions.stem: What is the correct order of the phases of mitosis?
options: Telophase, metaphase, anaphase, prophase
Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
Metaphase, prophase, anaphase, telophase
Prophase, anaphase, metaphase, telophase
questions.explanation: Chromosomes condense in prophase, line up in metaphase, separate in anaphase and reach the poles as nuclei re-form in telophase. Cytokinesis usually overlaps with telophase.

questions.stem: In telophase of mitosis, which event takes place?
options: Nuclear membranes re-form around the two sets of chromosomes at the poles
Chromosomes condense and the nuclear membrane begins to break down
Homologous chromosomes pair up and exchange sections of their non-sister chromatids
Chromosomes line up in single file across the middle of the spindle
questions.explanation: Telophase reverses prophase: chromosomes decondense and a nuclear membrane forms around each set. Pairing of homologues occurs only in prophase I of meiosis.

questions.stem: What is cytokinesis?
options: Movement of chromosomes to the poles along the fibres of the spindle
Division of the cytoplasm to form two separate cells after the nucleus divides
Division of the nucleus so that each new nucleus has a full set of chromosomes
Replication of DNA so that each chromosome has two identical chromatids
questions.explanation: Mitosis divides the nucleus; cytokinesis then splits the cytoplasm and organelles, by a cleavage furrow in animal cells or a cell plate in plant cells. Without it, the cell would have two nuclei.

questions.stem: What is the overall outcome of meiosis in one diploid cell?
options: Four diploid cells, each genetically identical
Two haploid cells, each genetically identical
Four haploid cells, each genetically different
Two diploid cells, each genetically identical
questions.explanation: Meiosis has two divisions, giving four cells, each with half the chromosome number. Crossing over and independent assortment make them genetically different. Two identical diploid cells is the outcome of mitosis.

questions.stem: In which phase of meiosis does crossing over occur?
options: Anaphase I, when homologous chromosomes separate
Telophase II, when four nuclei have formed
Prophase I, when homologous chromosomes are paired
Metaphase II, when chromosomes line up singly
questions.explanation: Crossing over happens while homologues are paired in prophase I, at points called chiasmata, swapping sections between non-sister chromatids. By anaphase I the homologues are moving apart.

questions.stem: During anaphase I of meiosis, what separates and moves to opposite poles?
options: Whole sets of chromosomes, which remain paired as bivalents
Individual DNA strands, each acting as a template for copying
Homologous chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids
Sister chromatids, which then become separate single chromosomes
questions.explanation: In anaphase I homologous pairs are pulled apart, which is the basis of random segregation, but sister chromatids stay joined. Sister chromatids separate in anaphase II, as in mitosis.

questions.stem: An organism has a diploid number of 8. Considering independent assortment only, how many genetically different gametes can it produce, and how many chromosomes does each contain?
options: 64 combinations, each gamete with 4 chromosomes
16 combinations, each gamete with 4 chromosomes
8 combinations, each gamete with 8 chromosomes
16 combinations, each gamete with 8 chromosomes
questions.explanation: With 4 homologous pairs, each lining up independently, there are 2⁴ = 16 combinations. Gametes are haploid, so each has 8 ÷ 2 = 4 chromosomes.

questions.stem: A cell with 2n = 4 is seen with two chromosomes, each made of two chromatids, lined up singly across the equator. Which stage is this?
options: Anaphase II of meiosis
Metaphase II of meiosis
Metaphase of mitosis
Metaphase I of meiosis
questions.explanation: Only 2 chromosomes (n) are present, so the cell has completed meiosis I. Lining up singly with two chromatids each is metaphase II. Metaphase of mitosis in this cell would show all 4 chromosomes.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares mitosis and meiosis?
options: Mitosis halves the chromosome number and gives varied cells; meiosis keeps it and gives identical cells
Mitosis involves two divisions and crossing over; meiosis involves one division and no crossing over
Mitosis occurs only in gametes; meiosis occurs in all the body cells for growth and repair
Mitosis keeps the chromosome number and gives identical cells; meiosis halves it and gives varied cells
questions.explanation: Mitosis is one division that produces two genetically identical diploid cells. Meiosis is two divisions, with crossing over and independent assortment, producing four genetically varied haploid cells.

questions.stem: Why is accurate DNA replication before mitosis essential?
options: So that each daughter cell receives half of the genes of the parent cell
So that the daughter cells differ from each other to increase variation
So that the cell can make RNA primers to use as its genetic material
So that each daughter cell receives a complete, identical copy of the genome
questions.explanation: Without replication each daughter would get only part of the DNA, and errors would cause mutations. Mitosis is meant to produce genetically identical cells, not varied ones.

questions.stem: Why is meiosis essential in organisms that reproduce sexually?
options: It repairs damaged tissue in the reproductive organs, keeping the gonads healthy over a lifetime
It halves the chromosome number, keeping it constant across generations, and creates variation
It doubles the chromosome number, so the offspring have more genes than either of their parents
It produces cells identical to the parent, so useful traits are kept unchanged in the offspring
questions.explanation: If gametes were diploid, the chromosome number would double each generation; meiosis prevents this. Crossing over, independent assortment and random segregation also make every gamete genetically unique.

questions.stem: Which process allows a cut on the skin to heal by producing new, genetically identical cells?
options: Crossing over in the cell cycle
DNA replication without division
Mitosis followed by cytokinesis
Meiosis followed by cytokinesis
questions.explanation: Growth and repair use mitosis, which gives cells identical to the originals, followed by cytokinesis to separate them. Meiosis produces haploid, genetically different gametes.
